# Game Animation Training 3

**LEVEL 3 \- Quadruped Documentation**  
Created by Adrian Nicklaus, last modified on February 10, 2025

## **🧠 Walkthrough**

Please refer to the sample files from

**L:\\LEMONSKY\\LSATRG\_GENERAL\\PRODUCTION\\06\_References\\05\_Anims**  
**\\GameAnim\_Training\\L3\_Locomotion\\Quadruped\\Walkthrough**

The hind legs (back legs) will always move first, followed by the front legs   
(delayed)

* When the hind leg is in a passing pose, the front leg will always be in contact pose

  ![][image1]


* With both front and hind legs moving differently, the translation Y of the hip and chest would also be different (during **contact**, the translation Y will be **almost at the lowest** while during **passing pose**, the translation Y will **almost be at the highest**  
* The **hips** will have a **bigger translate Y amplitude** compared to the chest 

## **👨🏻‍🏭 Workflow**

### **1️⃣ Set your Speed** 

* Referring to the sample file, we will be using an average speed of 60cm/s (2cm/f) set at 30 FPS  
* Input the speed into your global (world) ctrl

  ![][image2]


* Some clients will give the speed in cm/f instead of cm/s. If this is the case;  
  * Divide the speed by your FPS first  
    * 60cm/s ➗ 30 \= 2cm/f  
  * Set the value of;  
    * 0 ➡ frame 0  
    * 2 ➡ frame 1  
  * Set the tangent to linear and the curves to Post Infinity with a cycle offset

    

    ![][image3]

    

    ![][image4]

    

* Now, you will get the speed right on the global (world) and can mute it. You will need to unmute again when checking for sliding


### **2️⃣ How to Cycle**

* Do ensure that you have turned on the infinity in the graph editor


  ![][image5]\\


* Select the start and end points that you want to cycle and under the Pre Infinity and Post Infinity, choose Cycle


  ![][image6]

  ![][image7]


  ![][image8]


### **3️⃣ The Walk**

#### **Part 1 \- The Leg**

* Focus on a single leg first  
* Decide the contact pose key frame  
* When the foot is touching the ground, make sure the translation z is on linear

  ![][image9]


* To make sure the foot is not sliding, in this example, go to the contact pose at frame 0 and set the same key at frame 15   
* Select the key at frame 15 (contact pose) and on the y value bar, input the equation “ **\-=30 ” \[minus\]\[equal\]\[30\]**. Make sure 0-15 is on a linear tangent (this is so that when you unmute the global, it will not be sliding). At frame 15-17, the foot is a little bit not touching the ground, therefore, you can give it a little cushion on the translate z (Refer to Quadruped\_Part\_01 file for reference)


  ![][image10]


* Focus on getting a smooth arc on a single leg first during this phase (Do not put too much effort into fixing pops and sculpting the shape of the foot as we are gonna adjust the hip right after this)

  #### **Part 2 \- The Hip**

* Overall, the principle is not so much different from a human biped  
* During contact, the translation Y of the hip will be **almost at the lowest point** and during the passing pose, will be **almost at the highest point**

  ![][image11]


* Rotation Y (side to side rotation) ➡ will be following the foot motion 

     1 to 1

* Rotation Z (left and right tilt)        ➡ when the foot starts to come 

     into contact with the ground, 

     the hip will start to tilt up to 

     receive the weight

* Rotation X (up and down tilt)       ➡ the hip will tilt up when it starts 

     hitting the ground as it takes 

     the weight


  ![][image12]


* Now that we have adjusted the hip, return back to the foot and maintain the shape that we need

  ![][image13]![][image14]

  #### **Part 3 \- The Chest & Front Leg**

* Select the animation from the hind leg and copy it to the front. Offset the front leg key around 6 or 8 frames (this will depend on each and everyone), the key point is when the hind leg is doing a contact pose, the front leg will be at a passing pose. In the file example, the passing pose is at frame 8, then we will offset the front leg by 8 frames  
* Do the same with the chest; copy the animation from the hips to the chest and offset by 8 frames

  **Extra Notes**


* The overall chest movement does not move as much as the hip  
* The chest movement is more dominant on rotation Y(side to side) movement   
* For the scapula, make sure to raise it up when the foot is touching the ground as it receives weight. This will add the “heavy” feel to the creature.  
* The scapula counters the chest movement meaning that when the chest is lowered, the scapula will go up instead  
* From the front view, make sure the scapula not just goes up, but also outwards as the foot stretches to reach the ground to give a squash and stretch feeling

  #### **Part 4 \- Secondary Animation**

* For tail and ears, you can use the layering technique  
* An example for the tail, copy the rotation animation from the hip to the base of the tail  
* Repeat the process until the tip of the tail (Make sure to scale up the animation a little bit each time you copy and paste)  
* Apply the Keyframe Offset tool (select the tail from the base until the tip and input how many frames you want to offset the animation ➡ refer to Tips & Tricks 


  ![][image15]





  #### **Part 5 \- Finalizing**

* Continue to fix the leg movements (arcs, pops, etc)  
* Add more detail on the fingers (claw, etc)  
* Copy the leg movement from 1 side to another side (if you started with the left leg, copy it to the right leg and offset by 15 frames)  
* Select the curves of the feet’s  translation x and rotation yz   
  * On the y value bar, input the equation \*=-1 to flip the animation
